title: Plumthump and the Big Shadow
markdown:
A young ogre named Plumthump lived way up high in the Frostcap Range. His home was a cozy cave that always smelled of toasted moss and warm berries. Sharing his cave, and his yummy snacks, was Plumthump’s bestest friend, Luna the kitten. Luna was tiny, no bigger than a thumb. Her fur was as white and soft as moonlight, and her eyes sparkled like dewdrops. She loved to pounce. Pounce, pounce, pounce. She would chase sunbeams, bat at sparkly icicles very carefully, and sometimes try to pounce on Plumthump’s big gentle toes.

Plumthump’s cave was a happy place. You could hear the soft rumble of his laughter and the tiny jingle of Luna’s bell. But one evening, as the moon started to climb like a big shiny pearl in the sky, Plumthump saw something that made his big green ears twitch with a little worry. Outside his cave, by the whispering bluebell wood, a big shadow stretched. It was so wide and dark. It looked like a giant dragon’s wing, spread out in the evening sky.

A shiver, not from cold but from worry, tickled Plumthump’s tummy. A little knot tightened in his chest. His tummy did a flip-flop. He squeezed Luna close, and she purred, a tiny rumble against his big ogre heart. It was a warm vibration that usually chased worries away. But this shadow felt different. It felt like a puzzle too hard to figure out.

“Hmm, Luna,” Plumthump whispered, his voice a low rumble, as comfy as a warm blanket. “That shadow looks… rather dragon-ish, doesn’t it?”

He did not really think it was a dragon, deep down. But it looked like one, and things that looked like dragons often seemed too big and too strong for little ogres. He wanted to make the shadow feel small. He wanted to make it less scary. But he was not sure how.

Plumthump was not a scaredy-ogre. He would help lost baby goats find their mamas and share his berry jam with any squirrel who looked hungry. But sometimes things that looked very, very big felt too much for his young heart. That night the shadow felt like a puzzle too hard for even the best ogre to solve.

“We must go and see, mustn’t we, Luna?” he said, mostly to himself. The moon was full and bright, a friendly face in the night sky. The bluebell wood shimmered under its soft glow. He wanted to prove to himself that he was not too small for big problems. His knees felt a little wobbly, like jelly. If he did not go and see, the shadow might grow bigger and bigger until it covered everything. That would not be good for the bluebells, or for anyone.

And so, with Luna trotting bravely beside him, her little tail held high like a tiny flag, Plumthump stepped out of his cozy cave. He left the familiar smell of toasted moss and warm berries, the comforting rounded shape of his rocky home. They entered the bluebell wood. The flowers glowed with a soft inner light, their petals like tiny stained-glass windows. The air smelled sweet and earthy. The path ahead was patchy with moonbeams, and also with stretches of dark shadow that made Plumthump’s heart beat a fast thump-thump.

As they walked deeper into the wood, the shadow grew larger. It loomed and stretched. Plumthump tried his best ogre jokes, the ones that usually made Luna giggle.

“Why did the dragon cross the road? To get to the other side!”

But the big shadow just stayed big and quiet. He tried singing a happy song about sunshine, but the shadow seemed to make the song sound thin. The path ahead was a little unclear, winding through rustling bushes. Plumthump’s heart thumped a quick beat against his ribs. He almost wished he was back in his cave. He froze for a moment, his big hands clenched, his brow furrowed.

Then, just as Plumthump was about to scoop Luna into his big pocket and scurry back, a yummy smell wafted through the trees. Warm sweet dough, sprinkled with something that smelled like captured starlight and honey.

“Hello there!” a cheerful voice chirped.

In a little clearing bathed in moonlight was a tiny goblin with a nose dusted with flour and a wide friendly smile. This was Idris Buttonnose, the baker. He was pulling fresh warm moon-cakes from a little oven that glowed like a captured firefly. The cakes were round and golden, with little flecks of sparkly light on their crusts.

“Lost, little ogre?” Idris asked kindly, his voice like the jingle of little bells.

Plumthump, still looking wide-eyed at the enormous shadow, mumbled, “A little. That shadow…”

Idris followed Plumthump’s gaze, his own eyes twinkling. “Ah, the dragon shadow! Makes a grand shape, doesn’t it? Always puts on a good show.”

Plumthump’s eyes widened. “You see it too? You think it’s a dragon?”

Idris chuckled, a warm rumbling sound. “Indeed. It certainly looks the part. But it’s not a dragon, young sir. Not tonight, anyway. It’s just old Grimble Rock, catching the moon in a rather dramatic way. See how the moonlight curves around it, making a big wide shape?”

He offered Plumthump a moon-cake. It was warm and soft, and when Plumthump took a bite, it tasted like pure moonlight and the sweetest honey. “Oh,” Plumthump whispered, his mouth full. The problem was not a fearsome dragon. It was just a big old rock. A gentle warm wave settled his tummy. He felt a little silly, too, for worrying so much.

They did not hurry the next bite. Plumthump sat on a bluebell-edge stone and let Luna bat at a crumb. A moth rested on the oven’s warm lip. Idris waited, flour on his nose, while the shadow of Grimble Rock held its grand shape and did nothing else at all.

Idris had baked so many cakes, piled high on a little wooden cart. Plumthump loved his moon-cakes. He really, really loved them. He could eat them all himself, warm from the oven, with Luna batting playfully at the crumbs. But Idris had been so kind, sharing his delicious treats with a stranger. Plumthump looked at the warm golden cakes, then at Idris’s kind floury face. He picked out two of the biggest warmest moon-cakes, the ones with the most starlight flecks. He held them for a moment, feeling their gentle heat seep into his paws. He hesitated. He really wanted to keep them. They smelled so sweet. His paws felt sticky with the promise of sweetness. Then he remembered Idris’s smile, and how good it felt to be offered something so lovely. Slowly, carefully, he held them out.

“For you, Idris,” he said, his voice soft but clear.

Seeing Idris’s happy face made the ache feel much, much lighter.

With Luna now chasing a stray moonbeam that danced on the path, Plumthump waved goodbye to Idris. He walked back through the bluebell wood. The moon seemed to wink at him. The shadows of the trees were just friendly shapes dancing in the moonlight. The wobble in his knees was gone, replaced by a steady stride.

When Plumthump arrived back at his cozy cave, he felt a lightness he had not felt before. He pictured old Grimble Rock catching the moon in its beautiful hug, a natural wonder, not a monster. He remembered Idris’s smile, and the taste of moon-cakes, and the happy feeling of sharing. He settled down with Luna curled on his lap, her purr a soft rhythm in the quiet cave. The moonlight streaming in felt like a warm hug. Grimble Rock, outside, kept catching the moon. Plumthump did not go back out to check. He already knew what the wing was made of.
characters: Plumthump (young ogre of the Frostcap Range), Luna (moonlight-white kitten)
